newsitem.title: USA: Record U.S. soy crop possible, freeze hurts wheat.
newsitem.headline: Record U.S. soy crop possible, freeze hurts wheat.

text.p: The nation's farmers are set to harvest their biggest soybean crop ever and their second biggest corn crop but a spring freeze hurt winter wheat, the government said Monday in its first look at the new crops.
The big soybean and corn harvests projected by the Agriculture Department reflected the most widespread plantings by American farmers since the early 1980s.

The department estimated the soybean harvest at 2.6 billion bushels, compared with 2.4 billion bushels last year, and a corn harvest of more than 9.8 billion bushels, up from about 9.3 billion last year.

It said winter wheat, which will be ready for harvest in a few weeks, would total 1.56 billion bushels, and estimated the total wheat crop at 2.26 billion bushels and the cotton harvest at 18.5 million bales, both a bit smaller than last year.
Many of the projections could change drastically since weather over the next six months will have a big effect on the harvest.

"As long as planting and growing conditions support these yields, we have to expect big crops," said consultant John Schnittker, who said there was little chance for farmers to build domestic grain stockpiles in the coming year.

"From this point on, we're going to be trading (on) weather and the weather is a little dry in western Kansas," said Steve Bruce, grain broker for E.D. and F. Man International at the Chicago Board of Trade.
Prices for soybeans and grains fell after the reports.

Soybeans for July delivery tumbled 16 cents to $8.73 a bushel, July corn fell 5 cents to $2.83 a bushel and July wheat lost 15-3/4 cents to $3.98 a bushel, all at the Chicago Board of Trade. Trading was heavy.

Farm-gate prices for this year's corn, soybean and wheat crops were projected to be substantially lower than 1996 levels, which would encourage livestock feeders and food producers to use more domestic grains and also make the crops more competitive in world markets.

Large harvests would be needed to meet demand and replenish stockpiles. Domestic soybean stockpiles were forecast to shrink to 125 million bushels -- the lowest in 20 years -- and wheat stockpiles were pegged at a slender 465 million bushels.
Analysts said the most significant figures in the reports were the estimates for the winter wheat harvest and for soybean stocks.
Demand for U.S. soybeans was so strong that consumption was expected to run 118 million bushels higher than last year despite prices likely to average 63 cents a bushel higher.

A mid-April freeze hurt a promising winter wheat crop in southwestern Kansas and Texas and Oklahoma, lowering output by at least 200 million bushels. Based on May 1 conditions, the three states still would exceed 1996's drought-reduced crop.
Subfreezing temperatures in parts of Kansas and Nebraska at the end of last week brought fears of additional damage.

Farmers were speeding through corn and soybean planting at nearly double the usual rate. They intend to plant 68.8 million acres of soybeans, the largest total since 1982, and 81.4 million acres of corn, the largest since 1985, the department said.
Last year, U.S. farmers reaped 2.28 billion bushels of wheat, including 1.48 billion bushels of winter wheat, 9.29 billion bushels of corn and 2.38 billion bushels of soybeans.
The record soybean crop was 2.52 billion bushels in 1994, the record corn crop was 10.10 billion in 1994 and the largest cotton crop was 19.66 million bales in 1994.
